universe_context:
On February 28, 2026, the United States and Israel launched coordinated military operations against Iran, beginning a major regional war centered on Iran, Israel, U.S. forces and Gulf states. The opening strikes hit Tehran and other parts of Iran and targeted military infrastructure, air defenses, ballistic missile sites, nuclear-related facilities and senior political and security leadership. The U.S. campaign was called Operation Epic Fury, while Israel’s campaign was identified as Roaring Lion. The first wave began after sunrise in Iran, with large explosions reported in Tehran and thick smoke rising over the capital.

Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, 86, was killed in the attack. Iranian state media confirmed his death early Sunday, March 1, after U.S. President Donald Trump had publicly announced it hours earlier. State media said Khamenei was killed in an airstrike on his compound in central Tehran, in the Pasteur district, where the supreme leader’s offices and other key state institutions were located. Satellite imagery showed heavy damage at the site. Iran’s government declared 40 days of mourning, and some accounts also described a seven-day nationwide public holiday. At the Imam Reza shrine in Mashhad, Iran’s second-largest city and a major Shiite pilgrimage site, mourners raised a black mourning flag.

Trump wrote on Truth Social that “Khamenei, one of the most evil people in History, is dead,” and said the killing gave Iranians their “greatest chance” to “take back” their country. In another post, he said Khamenei had been unable to avoid American intelligence and tracking systems and that, “working closely with Israel, there was not a thing he, or the other leaders that have been killed along with him, could do.” Trump warned that “heavy and pinpoint bombing” would continue “throughout the week or, as long as necessary” to achieve what he called “peace throughout the Middle East.” U.S. officials described the operation as aimed at eliminating imminent threats from Iran, including its missile capabilities and nuclear program.

Israel said the strike had killed senior Iranian security figures in addition to Khamenei. The Israeli military said those killed included Iran’s defense minister, the commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and senior security advisers close to Khamenei. Named officials reported killed in the opening phase included Defense Minister Aziz Nasirzadeh, IRGC commander Mohammad Pakpour and senior adviser Ali Shamkhani. Israeli officials said the attack involved extensive air power; one account said about 200 Israeli warplanes participated. U.S. and Israeli officials said hundreds of targets were struck in the first hours of the operation.

Iran condemned the attack as a “gross violation” of its national sovereignty. The Iranian Foreign Ministry said military and civilian targets had been hit. The Iranian Red Crescent said more than 200 people were killed in strikes across Iran. Iranian state media said one strike hit a girls’ primary school in southern Iran, killing at least 85 children, according to a local prosecutors office, which said more children remained trapped under rubble. U.S. Central Command spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins said the United States was aware of reports of civilian harm, took them seriously and was looking into them. He said protection of civilians was of “utmost importance” and that U.S. forces would “never target civilians.”

Iran responded within hours with missile and drone attacks on Israel, U.S. bases and U.S.-allied Arab countries. Air raid sirens sounded across Israel. Iranian attacks were reported against Israel and against Gulf states including Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain and Kuwait. Jordan said it downed 49 drones and ballistic missiles threatening its territory. Israel’s emergency service Magen David Adom said a woman was killed in the Tel Aviv area by an Iranian missile strike. The conflict also affected maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and caused wider disruption to regional air travel, oil markets and shipping.

Khamenei’s death created the first Iranian supreme leadership transition since 1989. He had led the Islamic Republic for nearly 37 years after succeeding Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini. Born in Mashhad in 1939, Khamenei was a cleric and revolutionary opponent of Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi. After the 1979 Islamic Revolution, he became president of Iran in 1981 and survived an assassination attempt that badly injured his right arm. As supreme leader, he held final authority over Iran’s armed forces, security apparatus, judiciary, state media and major foreign and nuclear policy. His rule was marked by hostility toward the United States and Israel, expansion of the Revolutionary Guard’s power, support for regional allies including Hezbollah, the Houthis and Hamas, and repeated crackdowns on domestic protest movements.

Under Iran’s constitution, an interim leadership council assumed the supreme leader’s duties after Khamenei’s death. The council included President Masoud Pezeshkian, judiciary chief Gholamhossein Mohseni Ejei and a Guardian Council member chosen by the Expediency Council. Ayatollah Alireza Arafi was named to that role. The Assembly of Experts, an 88-member clerical body empowered to choose the supreme leader, then moved to select a permanent successor.

Just over a week after Khamenei’s death, the Assembly of Experts announced that a majority of its members had voted to appoint Mojtaba Khamenei, the late leader’s second son, as the Islamic Republic’s third supreme leader. Mojtaba Khamenei, born in 1969, was 56 at the time of his selection. A mid-ranking Shiite cleric, he had never held formal government office and had rarely appeared in public, but he had long been viewed as influential inside his father’s office and closely connected to the Revolutionary Guard. His appointment signaled continuity with the hard-line theocratic system built under his father.

The war continued after the succession. On March 17, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz announced that Ali Larijani, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council and one of the most powerful remaining officials after Khamenei’s death, had been killed in overnight strikes along with Gholam Reza Soleimani, head of the Basij paramilitary force. Iran’s Supreme National Security Council later confirmed Larijani’s death and said his son Morteza had also been killed. The IRGC confirmed Soleimani’s death. On April 1, an airstrike hit the Tehran residence of former foreign minister Kamal Kharazi, then head of Iran’s Strategic Council on Foreign Relations. His wife was killed immediately, and Kharazi died from his wounds days later, at age 81. A ceasefire took effect on April 8 after 40 days of sustained combat.
